A senior U.S. soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of assisting Russian ​intelligence, British police said on Tuesday, after the U.S. ‌ removed aircraft from British military bases over a separate apparent threat from Iran.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the arrest of the 41-year-old man was related to “allegations of espionage, ​which is of the utmost concern to the United States ​and our allies.”
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general ⁠of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, added: “The alleged conduct of a ​senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that ​insider threats are real and persistent.”
The arrest, which took place near the city of Gloucester, west England, on Tuesday, “is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism ​Policing investigations,” British police said.
But it occurred the day after ​the U.S. removed refuelling aircraft from a British airbase in the second such apparent ‌evacuation ⁠in three months.
Planes left the Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall, eastern England, on Monday, which, according to the Wall Street Journal, was prompted by a threat from Iran.
The U.S. in September withdrew ​bombers that had ​been used to ⁠strike Iran from RAF Fairford on security grounds over an incident police have linked to Iran, which ​has denied any links to attacks or incidents in ​Britain.
The soldier arrested on Tuesday was detained on suspicion of offenses under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, which relate ⁠to ​obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting ​a foreign intelligence service. Police said the country to which the allegations relate is ​Russia.

Porsche Recalls Cayenne and 911 in China for Two Distinct Issues
20 photos
Photo: Porsche
Over in the People's Republic of China, plenty of Cayenne owners must pay a visit to their Porsche dealers of choice to address a rearview camera issue. Additionally, the German automaker has identified a single 911 with potentially damaged center-lock wheel fasteners.
The Chinese State Administration for Market Regulation published both notices, with the SAMR using S2026M0136I and S2026M0137V to identify these campaigns. Suspect Cayenne models were produced between November 22, 2017, and May 27, 2025, whereas the center-lock 911 was manufactured on August 22, 2024, in Germany.
Internal combustion Cayennes hail from the Bratislava plant in Slovakia, which assembles the full-electric Cayenne line as well. As for the Neunelfer, the rear-engined icon is assembled exclusively in Zuffenhausen. Since 911 production began in 1964, the flagship sports car has been strictly tied to the German automaker's home base.
Regarding the Cayenne 's problem, blame the parking assistance software. Because of iffy software, the rearview camera image may not appear on the central infotainment display. Without a rearview image, there's a higher risk of hitting an obstacle or another vehicle while reversing.
Given the root cause, Porsche dealers in China have been authorized to install remedy software. That's all, but unfortunately, the update must be performed via the OBD-II port. An estimated 18,274 such vehicles from the suspect timeframe have been sold in the Chinese market.
Photo: Porsche This campaign has a US counterpart in the form of NHTSA campaign 25V896 from December 2025, which covers a massive 173,538 vehicles. Its scope covers the Cayenne, Panamera, Taycan, and 911, with model years ranging from 2019 through 2025.
As for the 911 center-lock wheel fastener campaign, the owner of that model could experience a wheel detachment at high speed. The single-car safety recall expands two earlier centerlock wheel recalls from November and December 2024. The earliest campaign included 68 units of the 911 and 718, with production dates ranging from November 8, 2023, through September 4, 2024.
The newly added 911 falls within that original production timeframe. In a similar fashion to the Cayenne's rearview camera issue, this one isn't exclusively Chinese either. In the United States, the campaign originally covered 1,851 vehicles. More recently, Porsche Cars North America expanded it by 548 vehicles.
The October 2026 expansion includes certain 911 variants, along with the 718 Cayman GT4 RS and the 718 Boxster-derived Spyder RS. In the United States market, owners are urged not to drive their vehicles until dealers inspect them.
As of November 2026, centerlock wheels are offered on the Carrera S MT Package, the GTS line, the GT3 line, and the Turbo S. The Carrera S presently starts at $156,200 before destination, and the MT Package adds $10,900 to the coupe's price. For some reason or another, centerlock wheels cannot be had as a standalone option on the Carrera S for 2027.
Via // SAMR

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the company’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.
That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.
Lucid lost sales with cars sitting in inventory
Napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He said that at the start of Q3, the company had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”
He said Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory .
So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.
In Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806 , down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.
Tesla went through “delivery logistics hell” in 2018
Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.
By Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.
Elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he said Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also launched door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.
It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk said Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers . Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.
Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.
Europe showed how fast a delivery fix matters
When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.
About a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the company preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.
It worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.
We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO said that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.
Electrek’s Take
This is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.
But it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.
Tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.

BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes. Now, BYD is taking things a step further with integrated solar power and a robotic arm that plugs itself in. See how it all works in action.
After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its new ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.
The Chinese automaker launched a new integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.
In 2006, BYD president and CEO Wang Chuanfu revealed his vision of “Three Green Dreams,” including harnessing solar power to generate renewable energy, storing that energy in batteries, and replacing gas-powered vehicles with electric ones that run on clean energy.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The new charging system is the “world’s first,” according to BYD, to integrate solar power generation, energy storage, Flash Charging, and robotic charging together in one solution.
BYD’s Flash Charging tech enables a vehicle’s battery to charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, essentially the same time it takes to fill up at a gas station. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.
BYD’s new Flash Charging robotic arm (Source: BYD)
The new robotic charging arm automatically locates the vehicle’s charging port, opens its cover, plugs in, and then removes it once the session is over.
By combining robotic charging with its Automated Valet Parking, BYD said the new tech goes beyond automated driving and parking to the charging process itself.
Once the vehicle is parked, the robotic charging arm automatically takes over and connects it to Flash Charging without the driver even touching the cable.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Michael Martinez (@mmichael_martinez)
Michaël Martinez, head of marketing at BYD France, posted a video (shown above) showcasing the new charging tech in action.
The integrated solution is built around BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging (SSC) system, fusing solar energy generation, battery storage, and its 5-minute Flash Charging tech. Together, the setup captures energy from the sun, stores it, and distributes it as needed.
Top comment by Zzyzx
Liked by 2 people
If they could tie this into a smart summon type of capability, where the vehicle communicates with the charger and moves the vehicle into the proper location for charging and then moves to a parking spot once charging is complete. Rental car fleets would benefit and so would those in shopping centers. There are so many possibilities and this looks far more mature that the old snake charging Tesla demoed.
View all comments
BYD has over 16 years of experience in the solar industry with a portfolio that includes solar cells, modules, and systems.
Its solar division, BYD Solar , does business in over 100 countries and regions. By using solar power, BYD said, the SCC system can operate independently off-the-grid.
The new technology is part of BYD’s wider Flash Charging rollout. By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy 6,000 Flash Charging stations globally.

Doug DeMuro Sold His Ford GT To Buy a Ford GT
8 photos
Photo: Doug DeMuro | YouTube
Doug DeMuro said he would do it. It was his plan right from the get-go. The sole reason for selling his Ford GT was to buy another Ford GT. Now here he is, showing his new car on camera. After eight years of owning a blue Ford GT, he now owns another blue Ford GT. And no, they aren't much alike.
The YouTuber bought the 2005 Ford GT in Midnight Blue from its original owner, automotive journalist Karl Brauer, eight years ago. Brauer had kept an impressive logbook where he documented every single event from his car’s life, even tracking every single fuel stop.
He chose it because it was basically the only Ford GT that he could afford at the time. Why was it cheaper than the rest? It had roughly 31,000 miles on the clock, which is a massive number for a collector car.
Unlike most supercar owners, Doug DeMuro didn't park it in a climate-controlled garage, hoping to cash in one day. He drove the wheels off it, adding 14,400 miles (23,175 kilometers) and pushing the total mileage to a whopping 45,800 miles (73,708 kilometers).
Photo: Doug DeMuro | YouTube His former Ford GT is powered by the hand-assembled 330-cubic-inch (5.4-liter) V8 with four valves per cylinder and an Eaton 2300 Lysholm supercharger. The setup pumps out 550 horsepower (558 metric horsepower) and 500 pound-feet (678 Newton meters) of torque.
Those are enough to make it flash from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in just 3.3 seconds and max out at 205 mph (330 mph). A six-speed Ricardo manual transmission sends power to the tarmac through the rear wheels.
DeMuro listed his car on his own platform, "Cars and Bids," with no reserve. After a week spent online, it went home with the one who placed the most generous offer: $540,000. The seller announced that what he gets from the buyer of his old Ford GT will fund a big portion of his new Ford GT.
Because it was a true driver’s car, it wore its history openly, as the listing disclosed rock chips on the nose, marks on the paint protection film, some clearcoat failure on one wheel, along with wear on the seats and scratches on the shift knob.
Photo: Doug DeMuro | YouTube Roughly three weeks later, here he is, showing up on camera to brag about his 2006 Ford GT Heritage Edition . Yes, "Heritage Edition" is the key here. Because he acquired the car through a private sale rather than a public auction block, the final transaction price remains confidential.
But just to get an idea about the potential price, this exact car sold publicly back in 2023 at the Barrett-Jackson 2023 Scottsdale Auction for $594,000, which is $54,000 over what DeMuro got for his former Ford GT. At the time, it had only 3,460 miles on the clock.
Thousands of miles were added in the meantime, all the way to 19,000 miles. In the very strict collector world, a high-mileage Heritage Edition drops significantly from the $1.5 million to $2.1 million prices commanded by sub-1,000-mile cars.
Higher-mileage Heritage Edition examples sit right around the $750,000 to $850,000 range on the used car market. With a high-mileage Ford GT Heritage Edition, Doug can now drive his new supercar guilt-free. The car belonged to Grammy-winning musician John Mayer.
Photo: Doug DeMuro | YouTube
Doug DeMuro’s new 2006 Ford GT Heritage Edition is one of only 343 units ever built. It is finished in the world-famous and ultra-popular Gulf Oil light blue and Epic Orange , paying tribute to the legendary Ford GT40 that won the 24 Hours of Le Mans back-to-back in 1968 and 1969.
The amusing part of it is that a few years ago, Doug DeMuro said that, with this livery, the Ford GT Heritage Edition looked like a clown. Well, now he owns a "clown."
Why did Doug DeMuro make the switch? Well, first, the Ford GT Heritage Edition is his all-time dream car, along with the Porsche Carrera GT, which he has owned for three years, and the Lamborghini Countach , which was first parked in his garage four years ago.
Despite owning the 2005 Ford GT for eight years, which is longer than any of the cars he has owned so far, Doug says he has never actually liked the color. In the meantime, the Midnight Blue gained traction among collectors, as blue with white stripes is one of the most sought-after combos.
Photo: Doug DeMuro | YouTube Furthermore, it was a good moment to sell his Ford GT. Over the last eight years, the collector market shifted dramatically, with prices going through the roof. So, it was the right time to cash in and use the money to buy a Ford GT that he actually liked the color of.
As for performance, the 2006 Ford GT Heritage Edition is a Ford GT is basically a standard Ford GT underneath, sporting the same engine, horsepower, torque, 0 to 60 time, and top speed.

New EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.
Across all new vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.
EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October. That’s up from 10.3% a year earlier and well above October’s industrywide average of 6.8%.
Tesla’s average selling price fell from September to $54,194, but it was still up 1.2% year over year. The Cybertruck helped push that average higher. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 1,914 Cybertrucks in October, its best month in more than a year, at an average price of $92,380.

source_document.body:
Most transportation management systems were built to answer a simple question: What’s the cheapest way to move this order? What they’ve been slower to answer is whether that plan will actually work once a driver, a dock door and a delivery appointment enter the picture. Then add in multiple dock doors, several delivery appointments, hours of service regulations and more, and there is a lot of complexity for the average planner to work through.
That gap is where FreightWise is placing its bet with Kuebix AI, an AI-backed TMS for small and mid-market shippers. Announced Oct. 20, the platform becomes the single system for every FreightWise and Kuebix customer, covering LTL, truckload and parcel in one place.
FreightWise CEO Chris Cochran sat down with FreightWaves at the F3: Future of Freight Festival in Chattanooga, a day after demoing the platform to attendees. His pitch was direct about who the product is for. “We’re focused 100% on the shipper,” he said, contrasting Kuebix AI with the many technology providers at the event that build for brokers.
One platform, one roadmap
The launch is partly a consolidation story. FreightWise acquired Kuebix in 2023 and has since operated two separate systems: FreightWise TMS and the Kuebix TMS platform. According to the company’s announcement, every customer will now work on the same technology, supported by one team and guided by one product roadmap. The practical upside, FreightWise says, is that features built in Kuebix AI reach every user faster.
Cochran described the starting point as a legacy platform with a loyal user base. FreightWise already ran a modern, native application for its managed transportation business, which gave the team a head start. They brought the features Kuebix users knew into that platform, and the result became Kuebix AI.
“Over the past year, our team has been rebuilding Kuebix with the same functionality Kuebix users have known for almost two decades, while innovating on the infrastructure, aligning AI with core features, and ensuring the platform has real staying power,” Cochran said in the announcement.
Thousands of users are already using Kuebix AI, and upgrades onto Kuebix AI will continue for SaaS only customers in the coming year.
Replacing the black box on multi-stop routes
The feature Cochran emphasized most is multi-stop truckload planning, which is where he sees the biggest gap between how TMS platforms work today and how planners need them to work.
In a traditional system, he explained, the multi-stop route is planned and then handed to a planner, who often discovers that it will miss delivery appointments. The planner can’t see why the system built the route that way and usually has no alternatives to choose from.
Cochran said he sees that as a legacy of optimization logic written years ago. “AI disrupts that in general because AI doesn’t need those algorithms,” he said. “It’s smart on its own.”
In Kuebix AI, the planner sees several route options on one screen, along with where each one is weak. One option might add miles to hit a delivery appointment. Another might cut miles to save cost but force a change to the appointment. The planner drags over the one that works and acts from there, whether that means resetting a customer’s expectations or flagging a retailer shipment where fees or damages could follow.
The point, Cochran said, is to keep planners inside the TMS. “Instead of them going away from the TMS when they have a bad route or a false positive, it allows them to do it right there.”
The underlying pieces highlight AI-driven service time builds delivery plans around hours of service, wait time, loading and unloading, and facility hours. Multi-stop AI routing then uses that data to flag whether a sequence of stops is feasible and recommends the optimal route. FreightWise says the goal is for the delivery dates shippers give their customers to hold up.
Integration without the IT queue
Integration is the other pain point Kuebix AI solves. A TMS is rarely the system of record for orders, Cochran noted, and in the SMB and small enterprise segments, IT resources are scarce and the systems feeding data are often old. Few people can work on them, and they may not support current JSON calls.
Kuebix Connect, a no-code middleware layer, is FreightWise’s answer. Cochran said the aim is to put control in the hands of the business user. That person matches fields between a WMS, ERP or other source system and the TMS visually, and maps the logic. Then AI within Kuebix Connect will monitor the connection on an ongoing basis.
“As the daily feeds come through, sometimes there might be bad data, or failures in feeds,” Cochran said, usually from something small like an incorrect character that keeps orders from coming into the system. “The AI embedded within Kuebix Connect will monitor that, will fix it and help you diagnose the source of that” so that freight doesn’t sit in the warehouse waiting on a data fix.
IT still has a role, he added. They’ll need to provide credentials and test for security, but the company isn’t relying on IT to make manual calls every time something breaks.
Dashboards that explain themselves
The third piece is Kuebix Intelligence, which the company describes as AI-backed dashboards for spend by location, carrier and mode that explain the drivers behind the trends, not just the numbers. Cochran tied this to end-to-end design not only of Kuebix AI, but FreightWise’s solutions as whole. Because rating, routing, freight audit and payment all live in one system, rather than having settlement data sit with a separate audit provider, he argued that the data feeding the AI is better.
“If your KPI is off, the AI tells you why it’s off, where did it go wrong,” he said, rather than a CFO waiting on a logistics analyst for an explanation.
The release adds a related capability. AI-powered freight audit exception resolution analyzes quoted rates against final invoiced amounts, identifies discrepancies, quantifies the financial impact and recommends carrier dispute strategies.
Why FreightWise waited
Cochran was candid that FreightWise wasn’t first to the AI conversation, and that it was a deliberate choice. By his own estimate, the company moved six to eight months later than he would have liked. But the management team was wary of a trend they saw across the industry. “We were kind of uncomfortable with this trend that people were putting AI for the sake of AI in applications,” he said, pointing to chatbots running on incomplete data and no context. For some of the early adopters, users would engage, but they were not longstanding value-driven AI solutions that solved real problems.
“We waited until we could make it operational,” Cochran said.
That philosophy shows up in the company’s term for its approach: operationally executable AI, meaning AI that solves real pain points. FreightWise CTO Chris Haarmeyer echoed the point in the announcement: “We didn’t set out to add AI for the sake of it.” The team started with problems customers and internal users raised, like delivery dates that ignore hours of service or scheduled appointments.
The company also addressed data security up front. “Customer data stays protected, it is never used to train third-party models, and every AI feature is opt-in,” Haarmeyer said.
Where Cochran draws the line
Cochran’s view of AI in logistics is enthusiastic but bounded. He named two concerns. The first is data quality. “You’re not ready for AI if you don’t have good data,” he said, warning that AI can hallucinate and reach false conclusions when it’s fed bad inputs. Shippers without a clean, single source of record, he argued, will be at a disadvantage to peers who have one.
The second is customer relationships. “AI is not here to manage your customer relationships,” Cochran said. He doesn’t want customers calling FreightWise support or an account manager and ending up talking to a bot. When a customer is in a pinch, he wants them talking to a real person.
He also isn’t positioning AI as a cure-all. Someone still has to sell the order, load the truck and deliver the goods, he noted. But he was firm that shippers who skip it risk watching their cost to serve drift out of control.
What to watch
For shippers, the proof will come in execution. The release says additional AI-backed functionality will roll out in 2027 and beyond, and the upgrade of legacy Kuebix users to Kuebix AI is actively underway. The priority continues to be ensuring new features are solving real business problems, easy integrating for shippers with their existing technology with AI to flag any errors, and prioritizing data to inform better decisions.

Kia opened orders for two new PV5 electric van variants, the PV5 Chassis and PV5 Cargo L2/H2, in the UK.
Kia expands PV5 electric van lineup
The PV5 is Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business. Built on Hyundai Motor’s dedicated modular skateboard platform, E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to enable “limitless possibilities.”
So far, the PV5 has mostly been available in Passenger and Cargo body styles with several different variations.
Kia added the PV5 Chassis , an open-bed model that can be converted into just about anything. In the UK, Kia is offering conversions through TGS Automotive Group, including lightweight tipper, Dropside, and Box solutions.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The PV5 Chassis is available exclusively with the long-range 71.2 kWh battery in the UK , which Kia said could offer a potential WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km).
For reference, the PV5 Cargo L2/H1, which uses the same 71.2 kWh battery, offers a WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km). Other markets will also have a standard-range 51.1 kWh option.
Kia PV5 Chassis Cab (Source: Kia)
The Chassis model is 4,610 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,935 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.
Its compact size and 5.5-meter turning radius, Kia said, make it easy to maneuver in city streets, construction sites, and other tight work areas.
Inside, the PV5 Chassis features two seats. Like other variants, it includes a 12.9″ navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.
Kia PV5 Chassis Cab Tipper (Source: TGS Automotive Group)
The Chassis model supports DC fast charging up to 120 kW, enabling the battery to charge from 10% to 80% in about 30 minutes. Using an 11 kW AC supply, it takes about 6 hours and 30 minutes to charge from 10% to 100%.
Payload depends on the configuration. Kia said the Dropside offers a payload of up to 633 kg, while the Tipper can carry 561 kg.
Variant | Battery | Basic Price (+VAT) | ZEVG | On-the-road (including ZEVG)
PV5 Chassis ‘Plus’ LR | 71.2kWh | £30,605 | £5,000 | £32,916
PV5 Dropside ‘Plus’ LR (conversion by TGS) | 71.2kWh | £36,600 | £5,000 | £40,110
PV5 Tipper ‘Plus’ LR (conversion by TGS) | 71.2kWh | £37,600 | £5,000 | £41,310
Kia PV5 Chassis prices in the UK by trim
In the UK, the PV5 Chassis is now on sale from £32,916 ($43,400) on the road, including the expected £5,000 ($6,700) UK Zero Emission Van Grant.
However, it’s an “incomplete vehicle,” as Kia describes it. The converted PV5 Dropside is priced from £40,110 ($53,500) on the road, including the ZEVG, while the PV5 Tipper starts at £41,310 ($55,000).
Kia PV5 Cargo L2/H2 (Source: Kia)
Kia also launched the larger PV5 Cargo L2/H2 in the UK. The new variant is 4,695mm long, 1,895mm wide, and 2,200mm high, with a 2,995mm wheelbase.
The taller roof opens up an internal cargo-area height of 1,815mm. It also offers a greater load capacity than the L1/H1 and L2/H2, with 5.2 cubic meters.
It’s available in three- and four-door configurations with the choice of two or three seats. The three-door versions have a maximum payload of 630 kg, while the four-door models have dual sliding doors and offer a payload of up to 600 kg. Both versions can tow up to 1,500 kg.
Variant | Battery | Basic Price (+VAT) | ZEVG | On-the-road (including ZEVG)
PV5 Cargo L2/H2 ‘Essential’ two-seat LR | 71.2kWh | £32,355 | £5,000 | £35,016
PV5 Cargo L2/H2 ‘Essential’ three-seat LR | 71.2kWh | £32,355 | £5,000 | £35,016
PV5 Cargo L2/H2 ‘Plus’ two-seat LR | 71.2kWh | £33,355 | £5,000 | £36,216
PV5 Cargo L2/H2 ‘Plus’ three-seat LR | 71.2kWh | £33,355 | £5,000 | £36,216
PV5 Cargo L2/H2 ‘Plus Walk Through’ LR | 71.2kWh | £34,425 | £5,000 | £37,500
Kia PV5 Cargo L2/H2 prices in the UK by trim
Like the Chassis model, the PV5 Cargo L2/H2 is available in the UK exclusively with the 71.2 kWh battery, which provides a WLTP range of up to 239 miles.
Inside, it features the same setup as the other PV5 variants, including a 12.9″ touchscreen navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display.
The base PV5 Cargo L2/H2 Essential two-seat starts at £35,016 ($46,700), on the road, including ZEVG.

2028 BMW Alpina i7 Shows Off Its Amber Running Lights
20 photos
Photo: SH Proshots
BMW Alpina is presently developing a new flagship electric model, distinct from the BMW-only i7. Previously teased with V8 muscle by its maker, the Alpina line will also include i7 models. This brown-painted test vehicle is one of them, and chances are that we are looking at the range-topping 70 xDrive specification.
Carefully camouflaged where it matters, the prototype resembles the facelifted i7. Amber daytime running lights, sporty wheels, and the revised front bumper give it a different identity from the BMW sibling. An electric Alpina might have been unlikely when the Bovensiepen family called the shots, but zero-emission vehicles are definitely in the offing after BMW acquired the rights to the Alpina name.
Devoid of makeshift exhaust outlets, the full-electric prototype stands out from the BMW i7 through its thin amber front lighting elements. The front lights follow the split layout of the current model, but the color differentiates Alpina from BMW. This is also the case with certain M Performance and M models, which feature motorsport-inspired M Yellow Lights.
The warm signature was previewed by the Vision BMW Alpina concept and the camouflaged V8-powered 7 Series prototype unleashed by the Bavarian manufacturer on its media portal at the beginning of November 2026. Said internal combustion prototype is anything but an M7 with extra luxury, but nevertheless, it successfully exceeded 300 kilometers per hour (186 miles per hour) at Nardo .
A fairly restrained way of recognizing the Alpina 7 Series and i7 from the Bimmers, the amber lighting is joined by a grille outline and lower bumper setup that closely resembles those of the V8 prototype. Being fully electric, the Alpina i7 does feature a few electric-only traits up front.
Photo: SH Proshots A pronounced chin section and sculpted openings to the sides of the bumper, just below the front lights, can also be seen. Instead of Alpina multi-spoke wheels, the design of the wheels featured here appears closer to what you get on Ms. The same design was spotted by the carparazzi on an internal combustion prototype, distinct from the one presented by the automaker on its media portal.
This, in turn, suggests a degree of stylistic commonality between the 2028 BMW Alpina i7 and the 2028 BMW Alpina 7 Series . On the other hand, the automaker may be using common development components to reduce costs. Whatever it may be, there's no denying the Alpina will have its fans.
Retaining the monolithic proportions of the 2027 model year i7 and 7 Series, the full-electric model should be viewed as the battery-electric successor of the Alpina G7. The existing i7 M70 xDrive provides a reasonable starting point for understanding what may be hiding under the skin.
Over in Europe, said model generates a massive 680 ps and 1,015 Nm. Activating M Sport Boost or M Launch Control ups peak torque to 1,100 Nm.
That's 671 hp, 749 lb-ft, and 811 lb-ft, respectively, which is plenty enough for blistering acceleration. BMW advertises a 0-100 kph sprint time of 3.8 seconds, which should be read as 3.6 clicks from zero to 60 mph. Its top speed is electronically limited to 250 kph (155 mph).
Although the i7 M70 xDrive remains on sale in Europe and other markets, BMW North America narrowed its all-electric roster for model year 2027. Instead of an electric flagship sedan, BMW North America is much obliged to sell you the 570-horsepower M760 xDrive. Obviously enough, the M division's S68 twin-turbo V8 is the internal combustion model's weapon of choice.

1969 Chevy Corvette Spent 35 Years Parked Until Someone Bought It. Can He Bring It Back to Life?
17 photos
Photo: Classic Performance | YouTube
This 1969 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray spent 35 long years in a garage on a lakefront property. The house was repossessed, and the owner wanted it gone. This is how it ended up in the hands of a classic-car miracle maker. Can he save it and send it back on the road?
The last inspection sticker glued to the cracked windshield dates to 1991 . This means that this car hasn’t been on the road since. Locked away behind a white sliding door, in an underground garage with access to the house on the lakefront property, is a sad sight to behold.
The Corvette Stingray was crashed in the front at some point. With its front end severely contorted, it was parked and never touched again. The owner was probably planning to fix it one day. But that day never came. So, two years ago, when his house was repossessed, he wanted the car off the property.
Parked in his garage, it sat with the fiberglass nose broken, and the bumper and grille badly caved in. The frame was cracked and the internals might have been pushed backward. The windshield is shattered, and the convertible top is torn, but the hidden headlight mechanisms seemed intact.
Photo: Classic Performance | YouTube The 1969 Chevy Corvette is finished in Can-Am White (paint code 972) over a red vinyl Comfortweave interior, with everything original. It sits on the original set of four factory 15 x 8-inch steel Rally wheels, painted black, but they should be Argent Silver.
The car has a trailer hitch, bolted to the rear bumper, as if anyone would tow anything with a Corvette. Probably the owner of this Corvette did. The speedometer was dislocated at some point and shows 34,829 miles (56,062 kilometers), but the man trying to rescue it guesses it’s 134,829 miles (216,986 kilometers).
The car is remarkably unmolested, retaining its original engine, date-code-correct alternator, Quadrajet carburetor, ignition, and correct tach drive distributor. The only piece missing under the hood was the spark plugs, which had mysteriously evaporated. The owner had no idea where they were.
The ‘Vette has the 350-cubic-inch small-block V8 with a four-barrel Rochester Quadrajet carburetor under the hood. The V8 pushes out 300 horsepower (304 metric horsepower) and 380 pound-feet (515 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Classic Performance | YouTube That is what makes it accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.1 seconds and max out at 122 mph (196 kph). A four-speed manual transmission, the purists’ favorite, puts the power down through the rear wheels. Back in 1969, GM was still light-years away from rolling out its first all-wheel-drive Corvette.
However, all those verbs about performance should be in the past tense, because the car doesn’t run, doesn’t drive, has the engine seized and the wheels stuck. Besides, the owner wasn’t going to let it go out without a fight.
He originally asked for $6,000, but the classic car rescuer who went to see it said he would by no means pay more than $3,000 for the beat-up, run-down, badly crashed Corvette. He dragged it out of its long-term entrapment and waited for the call from the owner.
He waited and waited until earlier this year, when the owner finally agreed to the transaction. So here he is, dragging the 1969 Chevy Corvette up on his trailer, with wheels stuck on the right side, leaving deep trails on the ground. Eventually, the one at the back breaks loose, but at a price: the tread on the tire is torn.
Photo: Classic Performance | YouTube The first stop is at the car wash as he is trying to wash off over three decades of abandonment in which this car collected dust instead of miles. Now, it looks miles apart from the car he found two years ago. Once he gets to the shop, he installs new redline tires that he bought on eBay, because there was no way the old rubber could hold air.
To finally break the engine loose and get it to start for the first time in over three decades, its new owner soaked the cylinders in Marvel Mystery Oil for roughly a week. Then, he rolled the Corvette down the trailer and positioned it at the top of a steep hill.
With the transmission shifted into fourth gear, he let the car gain momentum down the hill and repeatedly dropped the clutch. After four to five violent, sudden engagements, the seized engine finally broke free. A piece of painter's tape placed on the engine belt confirmed the motor was spinning freely again.
However, all he gets are a few pops out of the carburetor and exhaust. The compression test brings more bad news, but he is not the one to give up so easily. However, not all "Will it run?" videos end up with an exhaust pipe smoking out all the fury the car collected during decades of sitting parked.

One in six supply chain, logistics, distribution and wholesale professionals said their company experienced an incident in the past year in which supplier or customer information was exposed through an artificial intelligence tool, according to a new industry survey.
The findings come as businesses increasingly give AI systems access to sensitive commercial information, raising questions about how the technology handles confidential data belonging to customers and suppliers.
The survey was conducted by InstaLILY, which develops AI agents for distribution, and was fielded through Pollfish. Launched Oct. 9, 2026, it collected 250 responses from managers and executives at companies using AI in their daily operations. It found that 78% of respondents said their company’s AI tools could access customer pricing and margins, while 67% said the tools had access to supplier pricing and rebate information.
InstaLILY defined an incident as a situation in which supplier or customer data was exposed, shared or accessed incorrectly through an AI tool. The results reflect respondents’ reported knowledge and experiences, rather than independently verified data exposures. Also, the report did not assess the severity of the incidents, meaning the findings do not distinguish between minor internal mistakes and more serious incidents.
The survey also found that 63% of respondents said their company had been asked by a supplier or customer how it protects their information. For 30%, those inquiries had influenced a decision involving a software provider, vendor or AI tool.
“Speed means very little if a faster answer costs you a relationship that took years to build,” said Adam Isenberg, head of distribution at InstaLILY. “AI working in distribution should know that one customer’s contract price never belongs on another customer’s quote. Buyers should make vendors prove that before they sign.”
Despite the reported incidents, confidence in existing AI safeguards remains high. Eighty-seven percent of respondents said they were very or somewhat confident their AI tools kept supplier and customer information appropriately separated. However, 63% acknowledged some overlap between supplier and customer data across their company’s platforms, including AI tools.
The survey reflects broader concerns about AI security, going beyond just the logistics industry. IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report found that 13% of surveyed organizations had experienced a breach involving AI models or applications. Among those organizations, 97% reported lacking proper AI access controls. The report also found that breaches involving unauthorized AI tools, commonly called shadow AI , added an average of $670,000 to breach costs.
InstaLILY found that the most commonly cited obstacle to separating supplier and customer information was that existing AI tools were not designed with that requirement in mind, which was cited by 22% of respondents. Cost and a lack of technical expertise followed at 21% and 20%, respectively.
Nine in 10 respondents said their employers would be more likely to select an AI tool specifically designed for distribution and supply chain operations if it offered stronger controls over supplier and customer data. Meanwhile, 92% said data separation was a high or moderate priority for their company over the next year.
The report recommends testing AI systems against routine business scenarios, including whether a tool can prepare a customer quote without exposing confidential supplier pricing or contract terms. It also recommends establishing when human approval is necessary before AI systems act on information.
Why this matters
AI tools are gaining access to sensitive commercial information, including customer pricing, supplier contracts and rebate data. For logistics providers, distributors and wholesalers, a data exposure could damage relationships with trading partners and influence which technology vendors companies choose.
